title: Mounting Drosophila pupae for laser ablation and live imaging of the dorsal thorax
protocol: Place a piece of double-sided tape lengthwise on the center of a microscope slide, beginning about one-half inch onto the slide and ending with a small tab overhanging the edge of the slide.
Use a dull flat-ended probe to gently pry staged pupae off the side of the vial.
Very gently maneuver the flattest part of the probe underneath the pupal case.
Lift the pupa away from the vial, ensuring it adheres to the probe.
Carry the pupa to a microscope slide and place it in the region not covered with double-sided tape.
Use fine-tipped forceps to grasp the pupa between the anterior spiracles.
Place the pupa ventral side down onto double-sided tape near the center of the tape, leaving equal space anterior and posterior to the pupae.
Ensure there is enough lateral space to grab and remove the tape from the microscope slide later.
Gently grasp each pupa between the anterior spiracles using fine-tipped forceps.
Place the pupa down on double-sided tape.
Press gently on the posterior of the pupa to adhere it to the tape.
Evenly space pupae next to each other, leaving enough room for dissection.
Repeat the process for multiple genotypes, labeling distinct genotypes if necessary.
Arrange pupae with heads approximately level and largest pupa in the center.
Rotate the entire slide 90° so that anterior faces right if dissecting right-handed (left if dissecting left-handed).
Zoom in under a dissection scope so the pupae are very large.
Use extra-sharpened forceps to grab the operculum, gently pull it away, and discard it.
Press down the newly exposed inside area of the ventral case to the double-sided tape.
Gently insert one tip of the forceps between the case and the pupa, and slowly slide the forceps posteriorly.
Maintain the forceps at an angle parallel to the pupa, keeping the tip hugging the underside of the case.
Perforate/snip the case with the forceps once inserted approximately one-third to one-half down the pupal case.
Gently unwrap that portion of the case over the pupa and adhere it to the double-sided tape.
Reveal the dorsal thorax (notum) of the pupa.
Unwrap the remaining portion of the case on the opposite side (on the left-right pupa axis).
Adhere the unwrapped portion of the case to the double-sided tape.
Avoid puncturing the pupae during steps 10–12.
Discard and remove the pupa if it is punctured.
Continue with the next pupa if a puncture occurs.
Place two pieces of double-sided tape on top of each other on the lower half of the cover glass to act as a riser/fulcrum for the pupae.
Cut overhangs from the tape and attached pupae.
Remove the tape with attached pupae from the microscope slide.
Position the tape on the cover glass so that the nota of the pupa touch the glass, and the posterior cases rest on the riser.
Press down the side of the tape anterior to the pupae against the cover glass using the handle of forceps.
Trim any overhangs with scissors if necessary.
Drape a semi-permeable membrane over the pupae to prevent excess moisture loss while allowing gas exchange.
Carefully remove the double-sided tape with pupae from the microscope slide by pulling up on the tab.
Ensure the pupae are not harmed, and the tape does not curl back and stick to itself.
Gently lay the tape with pupae onto the cover glass so that the exposed nota of all the pupae are pressed against the cover glass.
Place the posterior ends of the pupae on the cover glass’ tape riser.
Do not press the tape down completely against the cover glass near the posterior end of the pupae.
Leave a small opening posterior to the pupae for air to enter and escape.
Use the handle of the forceps to gently press the pupa-containing tape against the cover glass nearest to the anterior side of the pupae.
Press the left and right sides of the pupae using the forceps handle.
Flip the slide over occasionally to check how much of the notum has been pressed down.
Drape a dialysis membrane over the opening posterior to the pupae.
Seal the membrane against the pieces of tape that have already been pressed down.
Cut away any overhanging pupal tape or membrane carefully.
Mount the slide on an inverted microscope for imaging.
Move the stage to aim the laser to the desired region of the pupa.
Align the stage so the border of red fluorescence is in the center of the frame.
Set the camera settings accordingly and save this single-frame image.
Begin taking a time series in the relevant fluorescent channel before wounding.
Ablate pupae with a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser focused to ablate in the same plane as imaging.
Visualize intracellular calcium using GCaMP6m expressed ubiquitously in the pupa.
Take baseline images before wounding.
Ablate the sample using a laser pulse energy of approximately 1 μJ to create a wound with a diameter of ∼50–100 μm.
Continue imaging the sample after ablation until the relevant biological phenomenon has been observed.
